title: Shared Ownership, and the Cycle That Never Releases

questions.question: When does a shared_ptr destroy the object it holds?
options: When the last shared_ptr referring to it is destroyed, that is, when the count reaches zero
When the first shared_ptr goes out of scope
When the program exits
When you call reset on any of them
questions.explanation: The object lives exactly as long as the last handle. That is what shared ownership means, and it is why no single owner has to be identified.

questions.question: Why does a parent and child that both hold shared_ptr to each other leak?
options: Each keeps the other's count above zero, so neither ever reaches zero
Because shared_ptr cannot be stored in a vector
Because the destructors run in the wrong order
Because the parent is destroyed first
questions.explanation: Reference counting cannot collect cycles. That is a property of counting rather than an implementation gap, and it is why tracing collectors exist in other languages.

questions.question: What does weak_ptr contribute to the reference count?
options: Nothing, it observes without owning
One, like a shared_ptr
It decrements the count
It depends on whether the object is still alive
questions.explanation: A weak link records the relationship without keeping the target alive, which is exactly what breaks the cycle.

questions.question: Why must you call lock() rather than dereferencing a weak_ptr?
options: The object may already be gone, and lock forces the caller to handle that
Because weak_ptr stores an index rather than an address
To increment the count permanently
Because dereferencing is only allowed on raw pointers
questions.explanation: lock returns a shared_ptr when the object still exists and null when it does not. The compulsory check is the feature, not an inconvenience.

questions.question: What is the rule for a structure with links in two directions?
options: One direction owns, the other observes
Both directions should own, for symmetry
Neither direction should own, use raw pointers everywhere
The direction with more objects should own
questions.explanation: Children are owned by their parent, and the link back upward is weak. Applying that consistently removes cycles by construction.

questions.question: When is shared_ptr genuinely the right choice?
options: When the lifetime cannot be tied to one owner, such as a cache entry or an object shared between threads
Whenever an object is used in more than one place
Whenever unique_ptr produces a compile error
Whenever an object is allocated on the heap
questions.explanation: If you can name the owner, unique_ptr with non owning references is faster and documents the design. Reaching for shared_ptr to silence a compile error is how cycles arrive.
